surface: signal delivery (core/agentmgr)
violation: RESTATED 2026-08-01 - the original claim is only partly true on this toolchain, and the untrue half was load-bearing. The entry said core/agentmgr signals `by PID with no epoch guard`. It does not. os.Process.signal dispatches to pidfdSendSignal whenever p.handle is non-nil (go1.26.5 src/os/exec_unix.go:84), and os/exec sets that handle via pidfd_open on Linux 5.4+. So the five call sites - go_agent.go:465 (SIGTERM), :492 (Kill), :562 (SIGHUP), python_agent.go:507 (SIGTERM), :533 (Kill); note the original entry listed three and missed the two Kill sites - deliver through pidfd_send_signal against a handle bound at fork, and return ErrProcessDone after Wait without sending. That is a STRONGER guarantee than procsig's: a handle cannot refer to a recycled PID at all, whereas an epoch check compares two numbers. WHAT REMAINS TRUE, and is what this entry now names: gapi's local signal safety is INHERITED from the Go runtime and nothing in gapi asserts, documents or tests that dependency. It lapses silently if p.handle is nil - a kernel without pidfd, or a Process that has been Released - in which case os falls back to pidSignal, a raw kill by PID, which is exactly the original hazard. core/procsig exists, is tested, and has ZERO callers inside gapi (its only consumers are in goblin), so the mechanism this entry funded is unused here. ORIGINAL VIOLATION: Local signal delivery has no start_epoch check and no pidfd_open/pidfd_send_signal guard, leaving the kernel-level PID-recycling ABA hazard open.
rule: research/global-uuid-based-process-identity DDR-5 (start_epoch as cluster-level pidfd; end-to-end ABA safety)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-08-01 - closed on two gates, neither of which is a comment. Part (2) was already satisfied: the bare-PID delivery path is the CRIU-restored process, tracked as GAPI-DIV-046, and that entry is resolved - adopt captures procsig.StartEpoch at adopt time and delivery goes through procsig. Part (1) now has both forms the exit offered. TEST: core/agentmgr TestGoAgent_SpawnCarriesPidfd starts a real GoAgent through the ordinary Start path and asserts this process holds a pidfd whose /proc/self/fdinfo Pid is exactly that agent's pid. The handle is read from the kernel's view of our file descriptors rather than by reflecting into os.Process, so a field rename cannot break the gate and an absent handle cannot hide behind one. STARTUP: Phase0Deps gains RequirePidfd, run before every other obligation because it is a precondition and not an obligation, and RunPhase0 fails closed on it; core/procsig.RequirePidfd probes by opening a pidfd on self, so a false negative cannot come from the target rather than the kernel. REVERT-PROVEN BOTH WAYS. The agent test was broken by calling Release on the started process - which is not a synthetic sabotage but the second lapse this entry itself names - and went red naming the pid and the hazard. The boot gate was broken by keeping the call and discarding its result, the failure mode where a check reports a fault and lets boot continue, and TestPhase0_RefusesWithoutPidfd caught it because it asserts nothing after the precondition ran, not merely that an error came back. Restored byte-identical each time. TestRequirePidfd_RealKernel keeps the success path exercised so the gate cannot pass by never being reachable. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THIS ENTRY'S OWN TEXT, found while closing it. Its violation says core/procsig has ZERO callers inside gapi; that stopped being true when GAPI-DIV-045 and -046 landed - core/agentmgr/adopted.go and core/agentmgr/checkpoint.go both import it. And the five call sites have drifted from go_agent.go:465/492/562 and python_agent.go:507/533 to :479/506/576 and :519/545. Both are staleness in the record, not new divergence. RESIDUALS, stated rather than solved. Phase0Deps.RequirePidfd is nil-skippable like every other field there, so a wiring that omits it silently loses the startup half and nothing asserts the wiring - the same trap GAPI-DIV-046's exit names about checkFileLength. It is a bounded residual because the TEST half is not nil-skippable and holds the line in CI unconditionally. goblin's half of that residual is CLOSED as of 2026-08-01: gapi was tagged v0.1.0-proto2c, goblin re-vendored it and set RequirePidfd in internal/supervisor/pid1_wiring.go (goblin pull request 22), and the precondition has since executed inside real guests - goblind completes Phase 0 in the Privileged VM Checks job with the check active. The correction is recorded rather than the sentence being deleted, because this entry was closed partly for keeping stale facts about itself and silently fixing them would repeat that. What survives is symmetric and unchanged in kind: nothing asserts that EITHER repo's Phase0Deps literal keeps the field, so deleting the line goes green in gapi and in goblin alike. An AST gate asserting the literal carries it would close both at once; goblin already has that pattern in core/consensus/fsm_operator_keys_caller_test.go. And the test proves the handle exists at spawn, not that every later signal uses it; a Release between start and stop would be caught only by running that same assertion again. PRIOR EXIT (2026-08-01 reopening, superseded by the closure above): REOPENED AND NARROWED 2026-08-01. Do not close this by routing the five child call sites through procsig: that would replace a handle-based guarantee with a weaker epoch comparison and change nothing observable. Close instead on the dependency being ASSERTED rather than inherited. Two things must hold. (1) The pidfd path is required, not hoped for: either a startup or doctor check that fails when pidfd is unavailable, or a test that fails if a spawned agent's process does not carry a pidfd handle - so a kernel or toolchain that silently drops to pidSignal produces a red build rather than a quiet return to the original hazard. (2) Any delivery path where gapi holds a PID NUMBER rather than a handle goes through procsig, because there the epoch check is the only guard available. The known instance of (2) is the CRIU-restored process and is tracked separately as GAPI-DIV-046; this entry does not close until (1) is gated. Documenting the dependency in a comment is NOT an exit - a comment cannot fail a build. PRIOR EXIT (2026-07-29 reopening, superseded by the restatement above): the stated SURFACE is 'signal delivery (core/agentmgr)' and the stated violation is that LOCAL signal delivery has no start_epoch check; core/procsig was built and is excellent, but core/agentmgr does not import it. PRIOR EXIT (2026-07-28): RESOLVED - core/procsig delivers via pidfd_open + pidfd_send_signal behind a check-pin-recheck start-epoch guard; typed ErrStaleEpoch (no retry) and ErrProcessGone; Identify() captures the locator (pid, start_epoch, pid_ns_inode); Linux-only by operator decision, non-Linux compiles and refuses (ErrUnsupported).

surface: agent process lifetime (core/lifecycle/controller.go, core/agentmgr/go_agent.go, core/agentmgr/python_agent.go)
violation: Every agent process gapid started was SIGKILLed roughly one millisecond after the supervisor declared it running. lifecycle.Controller.ApplyWithContext derived a start-scoped context (context.WithTimeout(ctx, c.WaitStart)) and both GoAgent.Start and PythonAgent.Start spawned the child with exec.CommandContext against it. os/exec installs a watchdog goroutine that calls Process.Kill on that context's completion, so the agent died the moment the start operation finished - the deferred cancel is function-scoped, not block-scoped, so it fired on ApplyWithContext's return. Downstream the only evidence was a later verb failing with 'agent not running', which is how this presented: TestPythonAgent_Reload reading state 'failed'. Originally recorded on 2026-07-28 as a CI-only, green-locally flake with an unexplained fixture death; that characterisation was wrong on both counts. The kill is deterministic and reproduces locally when the test is run in isolation against a freshly built gapid - the earlier 'green locally' readings came from a full-package run whose ordering masked it and, at least once, from a stale bin/gapid that predated the source under test.
rule: go-manifesto section 12 (the suite passes where the gate runs); ecosystem-manifesto (CI is a consumer like any other)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-07-28: GoAgent.Start and PythonAgent.Start now spawn with exec.Command; the process is owned by Stop, which sends SIGTERM and escalates on its own schedule. ApplyWithContext still derives a start-scoped context, but cancels it explicitly when Start returns instead of deferring to function exit, and lifecycle.Runner.Start now documents the contract the bug violated: the context bounds the start call and an implementation must not bind a spawned process to it. The reload path's exec.CommandContext at python_agent.go is deliberately left alone - that command is a synchronous cmd.Run whose lifetime IS the request. Artifacts: core/agentmgr/start_context_test.go asserts an agent keeps writing heartbeats after its start context is cancelled, and was confirmed to FAIL against the pre-fix code ('4 beats before, 4 after') and pass after; TestPythonAgent_Reload passes in isolation for the first time; full race suite green including test/adk (117.2s) and test/e2e (10.9s), with zero 'agent process exited unexpectedly' warnings where CI had seven. NOTE for the record: this defect predates the GAPI-DIV-026 exit watcher. Before the watcher the death was silent and the suite passed on a stale 'running' state - the whole ADK suite was green while every agent it started was being killed. The watcher did not break CI; it made a pre-existing breakage visible, which is exactly what it was for.

Triage on 2026-07-28 found none of the alerts call-reachable: every x/crypto CVE lives in golang.org/x/crypto/ssh or ssh/agent, and the build graph imports only chacha20poly1305, curve25519, hkdf, pbkdf2 and scrypt; CVE-2026-25680 is in x/net/html against a graph that imports x/net/ipv4, ipv6 and bpf; CVE-2026-40898 is HTTP/3 QPACK trailer expansion in quic-go/http3, and the control plane speaks raw QUIC streams demuxed by ALPN, never http3. It is not imported, and govulncheck's call-graph filter is what keeps it from failing the gate - which is the reason the gate is govulncheck and not a version-range scanner. surface: core/crypto/verifybinary.go and pkg/cli/security.go (agent signature chain)
violation: Signature verification could never succeed. 'gapictl crypto sign' signed the CANONICAL digest - []byte(crypto.HashFile(file)), a bare hex string (pkg/cli/security.go:38) - while VerifySignedBinary verified against the raw bytes of the .b3 sidecar (core/crypto/verifybinary.go:43), which Magefile.go:64 writes as hexSum+"\n". The two messages differed by one trailing newline, so no signature the shipped CLI produced could ever verify. The same function trimmed for the digest comparison and did NOT trim for the signature check, which is what hid it: 'if actual != strings.TrimSpace(string(hashData))' immediately above 'if !Verify(pub, hashData, sigBytes)'. Because core/agentmgr/discovery.go:349-357 gates agent start on this in production mode, the practical effect was that --production could not start ANY signed agent. Found by the 2026-07-29 documentation audit while checking whether the documented signing workflow actually worked.
rule: go-manifesto (test behavior at public interfaces; assume hostile inputs, use proven crypto only); ecosystem-manifesto provenance rule (one verification codepath)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-07-29: verification now covers the CANONICAL digest - Verify(pub, []byte(actual), sigBytes) - matching what the signer covers. Signing the digest rather than the sidecar's bytes is the sounder contract: it keeps the chain pubkey -> digest -> binary independent of how the sidecar is spelled, so a .b3 rewritten without a trailing newline still verifies against an unchanged binary. The doc comment, which had described the old (broken) intent as signing 'the .b3 file's bytes', was corrected to match. ROOT CAUSE OF THE GAP IN COVERAGE: no test ever crossed the two paths. Any test that signed and verified through a single helper would have passed against the broken code, because both halves would have used the same message. The new core/crypto/verifybinary_test.go therefore reproduces the CLI's signing form and the build's sidecar format separately, then verifies through the discovery path. Artifacts: six new tests pass; and, decisively, reverting the one-line fix makes three of them FAIL with the exact symptom ('a signature made the way the CLI makes them did not verify', 'a signature over the sidecar bytes was accepted') - confirmed by experiment, then restored. One test pins the contract against future drift by asserting that a signature over the sidecar bytes is REJECTED. Full gate: 'mage lint' 0 issues / 0 nosec, 'mage test' green. HOW IT SHIPPED WITH A GREEN SUITE - the most transferable part: production-mode signature acceptance WAS covered, by core/agentmgr/safety_test.go TestSafeToExecute_ProductionAcceptsValidSignature. It passed because its helper signBinary signed []byte(hash+"\n") - the sidecar bytes - which is what the verifier happened to check, and its own comment described that as 'the gapictl agent verify convention'. The test mirrored the IMPLEMENTATION rather than the CONTRACT, so it stayed green while the shipped CLI produced signatures nothing could verify. Fixing the verifier made that test fail, which is how the mirroring was found. signBinary now signs what 'gapictl crypto sign' signs, and its comment records why. The lesson generalises: a helper that constructs its own input by copying the code under test cannot detect a contract mismatch, however many assertions follow it. All eight safety tests pass with the corrected helper, including the tampered-binary and wrong-key negatives, so the contract was tightened rather than loosened.

surface: ENABLED agent metadata (core/agentmgr/discovery.go, the three runners, core/supervisor/supervisor.go)
violation: ENABLED was parsed and discarded. The agent-level Enabled field had ZERO consumers: decoded at core/agentmgr/discovery.go, declared on core/adk/meta/meta.go, and never carried onto a constructed agent - which is why Describe() had no key for it and the supervisor's desc map could not consult it. core/supervisor/supervisor.go admitted this in a comment ('We should verify enabled? implicit enabled for now.'). Meanwhile docs/configuration.md, docs/features.md and docs/agent-examples.md all told operators that ENABLED = False prevents an agent from loading. It did nothing. Found by the 2026-07-29 documentation audit.
rule: go-manifesto (explicit over clever; fail loudly at boundaries); ecosystem-manifesto (documented behaviour is a contract)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-07-29 by honouring it (operator decision; the alternative was removing it from the schema and the docs). Plumbed across four seams: discovery resolves it, each runner carries it with SetEnabled/Enabled accessors set post-construction through the enabledSetter interface - matching the RunIDSetter idiom rather than adding a fourth positional argument to three already-long constructors - and the supervisor skips the three auto-start paths for a disabled agent. SEMANTICS: systemd's. A disabled agent is still discovered, registered and visible to 'gapictl agent status', and can still be started explicitly through the lifecycle verbs; only automatic start is skipped. THE DANGEROUS PART WAS THE DEFAULT, and getting it wrong would have been catastrophic: Go agents do not emit an 'enabled' key at all (verified against test/adk/fixtures/go/hash_agent/main.go, whose describe carries only id/type/version/language/description/capabilities), so a plain bool would have unmarshalled their silence as false and DISABLED EVERY GO AGENT IN THE SYSTEM. The field is therefore *bool: nil means absent means enabled, and only an explicit "enabled": false disables. agentmgr.AgentEnabled treats any type not carrying the flag as enabled, so a future runner cannot become silently un-startable. A second, self-inflicted trap was caught by the tests: the struct comment claimed a default of true while relying on a bool zero value, which is false; every constructor now sets it explicitly. Artifacts: four new tests in core/agentmgr/enabled_test.go covering absent-means-enabled, explicit-false-disables, all three runner types defaulting to enabled and honouring SetEnabled, and the unknown-type fallback; 'mage lint' 0 issues / 0 nosec; 'mage test' green under -race.

surface: core/agentmgr/schedule.go parseSystemdSchedule
violation: All three systemd-style timer prefixes are aliases for the same behaviour. parseSystemdSchedule matches OnUnitActiveSec=, OnBootSec= and OnStartupSec=, strips whichever prefix matched, parses the remaining duration, and returns an IntervalSchedule in every case - the prefix itself is discarded. So OnBootSec=1m does not run once, one minute after boot; it runs every minute forever, which is what OnUnitActiveSec=1m means. OnStartupSec is the same. The doc comment on ParseSchedule and docs/features.md both described the systemd semantics, so an operator declaring SCHEDULE = "OnBootSec=1h" for a once-per-boot task got an hourly job instead - a silent behavioural difference, not an error. Discovery's own default for a timer with no SCHEDULE is OnUnitActiveSec=60s, which is the only spelling whose name currently matches what it does.
rule: go-project-manifesto section 4 (deterministic behaviour by default; an interface that accepts a name must honour it or reject it); cooperative-ecosystem-manifesto section 3 (systemd-compatible spellings carry systemd semantics or are not offered)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-07-29 by implementing the two missing semantics rather than rejecting the prefixes, so a systemd-compatible spelling carries systemd behaviour. A new OnceSchedule fires a single time at a fixed instant and then returns the ZERO time; the Schedule interface documents zero as 'exhausted' and TimerAgent.run stops on it instead of busy-waiting. OnStartupSec anchors to the parse instant, OnBootSec to the system boot, read from unix.Sysinfo rather than /proc/uptime so it works before the PID-1 early mount phase; non-Linux builds return time.Now, degrading OnBootSec to OnStartupSec, which is announced in the doc comment rather than silent. The prefix table now carries each prefix's anchor as data, so adding one without deciding its anchor is a compile-time hole rather than a silent alias - that omission is what produced the bug. A missed elapse point fires immediately, once (the run loop clamps a negative delay to zero), matching systemd's monotonic-timer behaviour rather than cancelling. ParseScheduleAt takes now and boot injected so the relative forms are testable without waiting on a real clock. ARTIFACTS: core/agentmgr/schedule_semantics_test.go asserts fire COUNT and fire INSTANT per prefix - OnUnitActiveSec repeats, the other two fire exactly once, and OnBootSec=45m resolves to 15m from a now that is 30m past boot, proving the anchor. End to end, test_timer.sh runs an OnStartupSec=3s agent for 11s and requires EXACTLY one fire plus a 'timer schedule exhausted' log line. Flipping the two prefixes back to repeating makes both the unit tests and the harness fail ('OnStartupSec=3s fired 3 times in 11s, want exactly 1').

surface: core/agentmgr/discovery.go agent construction, core/agentmgr/timer_agent.go, pkg/cli/templates/go_timer.tmpl
violation: Only PYTHON timers are scheduled. discovery.go routes to NewTimerAgent when meta.Type == "timer" AND the path ends in .py or .py.timer; every other timer falls through to NewGoAgent, which contains no reference to a schedule at all. TimerAgent.execute confirms the asymmetry - it always spawns ta.pyRunner, so the scheduler has no way to fire a binary. The supervisor's timer auto-start path keys on desc["type"] == "timer" and calls ActionStart, so a Go timer starts exactly once, at discovery, and never fires again; its declared SCHEDULE is read into the describe map and then dropped. gapictl agent new <name> --type timer defaults to Go and scaffolds precisely this: pkg/cli/templates/go_timer.tmpl emits "schedule": "OnUnitActiveSec=60s" in its metadata and a start() that prints "Timer triggered". The scaffolded agent therefore appears to work - it runs once - while never honouring the interval it advertises. Separately, TimerAgent.execute bounds each fire with a hardcoded 30-second context timeout, undocumented anywhere: a scheduled backup or report that runs longer is SIGKILLed mid-write with only a 'timer execution failed' log line.
rule: go-project-manifesto section 4 (deterministic behaviour by default); section 6 (behaviour at the public interface is the contract - agent new is a public interface and must not scaffold a broken agent); cooperative-ecosystem-manifesto section 2 (the two ADKs have identical semantics)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-07-29 by giving binary agents the same scheduling Python ones have, rather than rejecting TYPE=timer on a non-Python agent - the dual-ADK parity claim is load-bearing and worth keeping. Scheduling was never language-specific; only the FIRE was. TimerAgent gained a lang field and a fireCommand seam: Python modules go through the ADK runner, an executable is run directly, which is exactly what its main does when not asked to --describe. NewBinaryTimerAgent is a separate constructor rather than a widened signature, so existing call sites are untouched and the choice is explicit at the point of construction. Discovery now routes meta.Type == "timer" to the scheduler for BOTH ADKs; the isPython test that used to gate it selects the constructor instead. The gapictl go_timer.tmpl needed no change - it already prints and exits, which is the correct shape for a fire. Also fixed while here: execute now derives its timeout context from the run loop's context rather than context.Background, so stopping a timer cancels a fire in flight instead of leaving it to run out the full 30 seconds; that also cleared a gosec G118 the new code surfaced. ARTIFACTS: test_timer.sh builds a real Go timer fixture alongside the Python one and requires both to fire at least four times in an 11-second window - observed 'triggered=11 completed=11 python=5 go=5'. Restoring the isPython gate makes it fail with 'expected at least 8 triggers in 11s across two timers, got 0'.

surface: core/config/config.go Load (viper AutomaticEnv + Unmarshal)
violation: The RUNTIME_ environment override works for only SOME config keys, and fails SILENTLY for the rest. Load registers viper.SetDefault for transport.type/address/insecureSkipVerify, metrics.*, logging.* and timeouts.*, then relies on AutomaticEnv plus Unmarshal. viper's Unmarshal does not consult AutomaticEnv for a key it has never seen, so every key WITHOUT a registered default is unreachable from the environment. Empirically, with all six variables exported: RUNTIME_LOGGING_LEVEL and RUNTIME_METRICS_ENABLED apply, while RUNTIME_SUPERVISOR_PID1MODE, RUNTIME_SUPERVISOR_PRODUCTIONMODE, RUNTIME_SECURITY_VERIFYKEY and RUNTIME_TRANSPORT_TLSCERT are all dropped and the fields keep their zero values. The affected set is every supervisor.* key (productionMode, pid1Mode, noEarlyMounts, watchdog.*, shutdown.*), security.verifyKey, and transport.tlsCert/tlsKey/tlsCa. This is a security-relevant silent downgrade in both directions: an operator who sets RUNTIME_SUPERVISOR_PRODUCTIONMODE=true gets a daemon running WITHOUT production mode and without signature enforcement, and no error; one who sets RUNTIME_TRANSPORT_TLSCERT gets the auto-generated self-signed certificate. security.verifyKey happens to survive only because supervisor.go carries a separate os.Getenv("RUNTIME_VERIFY_KEY") fallback under a different variable name. docs/configuration.md, docs/config-example.md and nix/module.nix all state or assume that any key can be set from the environment.
rule: go-project-manifesto section 4 (deterministic behaviour by default; no hidden global state); section 9 (fail loudly at boundaries - a rejected override is a boundary failure and must not be silent); cooperative-ecosystem-manifesto section 5 (configuration surfaces are uniform or explicitly documented as partial)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-07-29 by deriving the bindings from the Config struct rather than listing keys - the gap was exactly the keys nobody thought to list, so a list would reproduce it. bindEnvOverrides walks the tree by mapstructure tag and calls BindEnv on every scalar leaf, passing the environment variable name EXPLICITLY (EnvKeyFor) so the binding does not depend on how viper composes a prefix with a key replacer. Maps are skipped and documented as config-file only: logging.loki.labels has no single-variable spelling. A field added later is reachable because it exists. surface: test/test_timer.sh, agents/python/timers/tick.py.timer
violation: 'mage testTimer' is red and has been. Three independent defects in the harness, none of which the exit code distinguishes. (1) The script hardcodes absolute /nix/store paths into PATH, pinning go-1.25.4 while the dev shell now pins Go 1.26 - a hermeticity violation of exactly the kind 'mage doctor' exists to catch, and it rots on every toolchain bump. (2) It exports RUNTIME_AGENTS_DIR, which is read by NOTHING; the discovery variable is RUNTIME_AGENT_PATH (core/config/agent_paths.go). The agents directory is therefore found only incidentally through the dev-build search paths, or not at all. (3) The config it generates uses transport.certFile and transport.keyFile, the silently-dropped spellings - the same defect corrected in config/config.yaml - so the harness configures no TLS and the daemon falls back to a generated self-signed certificate. Separately, agents/python/timers/tick.py.timer declares no ID, so it registers under the literal agent id "unknown". Observed behaviour with RUNTIME_AGENT_PATH set correctly and only tick.py.timer on the path: SCHEDULE=OnUnitActiveSec=5s produced ONE fire in 13 seconds where the interval implies two, and the log carries a 'timer agent stopped' for it; across the full fixture directory every timer logs 'timer agent started' TWICE per supervisor boot. The scheduler is not simply idle - something is stopping and restarting timers, and the harness's 15-second window cannot tell that apart from a schedule that never fired.
rule: go-project-manifesto section 11 (gates are hermetic and runnable from a clean shell); section 6 (a test asserts behaviour at the public interface, and a green/red signal must mean one thing); build-environment.md (no absolute store paths in checked-in scripts)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-07-29. The ROOT CAUSE was not the harness: TimerAgent.execute invoked the Python runner without --type, so the runner defaulted to "service" and took the service path - AgentWrapper.start ran _await_ready, which looks for a live start thread, new non-daemon threads or an open port, found none for a timer body, and spun to its full 20-second deadline; main() then entered 'while True: sleep(0.25)' and never exited. cmd.Run therefore blocked until the 30-second execution deadline and the next fire never came. Measured directly: 'python3 runner.py --module tick.py.timer --start' hung past a 45-second timeout (exit 124); with --type timer it now returns in 0.038s, exit 0. FIX: --type defaults to None and falls back to the module's own TYPE, so an omitted flag cannot silently reclassify a timer as a service; AgentWrapper carries a oneshot flag for timer and oneshot types, runs start() synchronously without the readiness poll (for a one-shot, ready and finished are the same event), and main() skips the supervision loop; TimerAgent.execute passes --id and --type timer. A service still blocks as before (verified: exit 124 under an 8-second timeout). tick.py.timer gained an explicit ID - it had been registering as the literal agent id "unknown". test_timer.sh rewritten: inherits PATH from the dev shell, uses RUNTIME_AGENT_PATH plus RUNTIME_SKIP_SYSTEM_AGENTS against a fixture directory it creates, and asserts a FIRE COUNT and that triggers == completions, so a fire that blocks is a failure. Artifacts: 'triggered=5 completed=5 agent-output=5' in an 11s window at a 2s interval; with the supervision loop restored the same test reports 'triggered=1 completed=0' and FAILS, which the old substring assertion passed. CORRECTION to this entry's original text: the doubled 'timer agent started' was two DIFFERENT log lines, one from timer_agent.go and one from supervisor.go, not a double start.

surface: pkg/cli/security.go signCmd
violation: 'gapictl crypto sign' emitted a signature that nothing could verify. It hashed the file, signed the canonical digest, and wrote only <file>.sig - never the <file>.b3 digest sidecar. crypto.VerifySignedBinary reads the .b3 FIRST and returns 'reading digest' before the signature is examined, so a file signed with the documented command failed verification outright, and production-mode discovery rejected it. No other CLI verb writes a .b3 for an arbitrary path either: the Magefile writes them for gapid and gapictl, and 'gapictl agent build' writes them for scaffolded Go agent directories, so an operator signing a hand-built agent binary had no supported way to produce the missing half. Observed: sign a copy of gapictl, then 'gapictl agent verify' reports 'No .b3 file found' while the .sig sits beside it. docs/features.md and docs/getting-started.md both documented sign-then-verify as a complete workflow.
rule: go-project-manifesto section 9 (fail loudly at boundaries - emitting half a provenance pair is a silent boundary failure); cooperative-ecosystem-manifesto section 4 (provenance artifacts are produced and consumed through one codepath)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-07-29. signCmd now writes <file>.b3 as hexSum+"\n" - byte-identical to what Magefile.go emits - before writing the .sig, and reports both paths. Signing is the only operation that already computes the digest, so it is the correct place to record it. Artifact: test/test_integrity.sh signs a freshly built binary agent with nothing but 'gapictl crypto sign', and production-mode discovery starts it while rejecting its unsigned twin; reverting core/crypto/verifybinary.go to the GAPI-DIV-032 behaviour makes that same test fail with 'signed agent did not register'.

surface: test coverage of parsers and wire decoders
violation: No fuzz target exists anywhere in the repo. `grep '^func Fuzz' **/*_test.go` returns zero, and there is no testdata/fuzz/ corpus. GAPI-DIV-013 added the Fuzz target and its exit honestly describes it as a 'loud no-op at zero targets', so that entry is correctly closed - this is the work it left. The manifesto requires fuzzing the hostile boundaries: parsers, decoders, anything that eats wire bytes or operator input. Unfuzzed surfaces that qualify: core/schema/validator.go (agent manifest validation, 324 lines), core/agentmgr/schedule.go (systemd-style timer expression parser accepting operator strings), the agent stdout decoder at core/agentmgr/go_agent.go:581 and python_agent.go:610 (JSON from a supervised process into map[string]any), and core/crypto capability-token decode.
rule: go-project-manifesto (fuzz the hostile boundaries with native go test -fuzz; seed via f.Add plus a checked-in testdata/fuzz corpus; every crasher minimized and committed)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-08-01. Nine Fuzz targets across the four named surfaces, a committed 29-file corpus, and `mage fuzz` reporting nine targets instead of the loud no-op. Targets: FuzzValidateCPULimit, FuzzValidateMemoryLimit, FuzzValidateSchedule, FuzzParseVersion and FuzzValidateAgentDescribe (core/schema); FuzzParseScheduleAt and the two streamControl decoders (core/agentmgr); FuzzVerifyCapabilityToken (core/crypto). Each additionally fuzzed 60s beyond the gate's 10s, 6.3M to 53.4M execs, no further crashers. EACH TARGET ASSERTS AN INVARIANT, not merely absence of panic: parsers are total and return exactly one of value-or-error; where a round trip exists it is stable; the token verifier rejects only through its five exported sentinels, because errors are data and an untyped error escaping there leaves callers branching on strings; and the stdout decoder is CONTAINED - read-only with respect to supervisor bookkeeping, since a child able to flip those fields by writing to its own stdout could talk the supervisor out of supervising it. Determinism was a constraint, not an afterthought: ParseScheduleAt with pinned clocks rather than ParseSchedule, and a pinned key, resolver and now for the token. A crasher that cannot be replayed from its seed is worthless. TWO REAL DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED. ValidateCPULimit accepted NaN, Inf and +Inf: ParseFloat returns them without error and the guard was `val <= 0`, against which NaN compares false and +Inf compares greater. ValidateMemoryLimit accepted counts that overflow int64 once multiplied to bytes, and parseLimits computes that product in int64, so it wrapped and handed cgroups a NEGATIVE limit. Both found by the invariants at seed execution rather than by mutation - recorded plainly because it bears on what fuzzing bought: the mutator was never going to type "NaN", and the value was in being forced to state what acceptance MEANS. A THIRD FIX, decided by the operator: a repeating interval that cannot advance is rejected. OnUnitActiveSec=-1s and a raw -5s produced a timer the run loop clamps to zero delay, so it spun rather than fired late; zero is rejected on the same reasoning. The one-shot forms are untouched - an elapse point in the past fires once, late, per GAPI-DIV-036. A CLAIM THAT DID NOT SURVIVE CHECKING, kept so it is not re-derived: the fuzz report said "@every -1s" yields a negative constant delay. It does not. robfig's Every() clamps any duration below one second UP to one second (vendor constantdelay.go:15), so it is a one-second interval and advances. A first version of the fix probed the cron branch for non-advancement, which could never fire; that probe was removed, because dead code in a validator is worse than an absent check - the next reader trusts it. The corpus seed asserting that defect was renamed to record the clamping instead. RESIDUAL, folded in rather than opened separately because it is a known and commented structural duplication rather than a defect: schema.ValidateSchedule's cron branch does NO cron parsing. It rejects a `key=value` with an unknown prefix and otherwise accepts anything non-empty, so "hello" and "not a cron at all" both validate and then fail at runtime in agentmgr. The source comment names the cause: agentmgr imports schema (discovery.go:26) and schema does not import agentmgr, so schema cannot call the real parser and the logic was duplicated instead. Fixing it means duplicating a cron parser into schema or restructuring the dependency - an architecture decision, not a fuzz fix. THIS WORK WIDENED IT BY TWO CASES: ValidateSchedule still accepts OnUnitActiveSec=-1s and OnUnitActiveSec=0s, which agentmgr now rejects, so the validator says yes to two more things the runtime refuses. Failing at start beats spinning, but the divergence is wider than it was. WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS SILENTLY FALSE AGAIN: `mage fuzz` runs each target for a bounded 10s and passes when nothing is found, so the gate proves the targets EXIST and run, not that they still assert anything - an invariant weakened to `err != nil || true` would keep the count at nine and stay green. The corpus is the real regression surface, and it is only as good as the seeds committed to it. Separately, a fifth surface was found while fixing the second defect and is tracked as GAPI-DIV-049: validated resource limits can silently become NO limit.

surface: core/subreaper/subreaper_linux_test.go, core/subreaper/subreaper_diag_linux_test.go, core/subreaper/subreaper_linux.go (ReapLoop)
violation: TestReapLoop_DrainsPreexistingZombies is flaky. It failed in CI run 30542246977 (https://github.com/goppydae/gapi/actions/runs/30542246977) with "subreaper_linux_test.go:129: pre-existing zombie 28560 not drained", on a pull request whose only change was divergence.jsonl - so nothing in the diff can account for it. Its three preceding CI runs that day passed. NOT REPRODUCED LOCALLY: 40 runs of the test alone and 40 runs of the whole package, both clean, 80 total under -race; a 150-run pass under GOMAXPROCS=2 with CPU contention was in flight when this entry was opened. The hypothesis below is therefore unconfirmed and recorded as a hypothesis. Mechanism ruled OUT: a SIGCHLD lost before signal.Notify registers cannot alone explain it, because ReapLoop drains once on entry and again on a 500ms ticker against the test's 3s deadline, giving roughly six independent chances. Leading hypothesis: ReapLoop drains with syscall.Wait4(-1, ...), which reaps ANY child, and neither test joins the goroutine it starts - TestReapLoop_ReapsOrphanWithStatus runs first in the same binary and its `defer cancel()` signals shutdown without waiting for the loop to return, so that loop can outlive its test and swallow this test's orphan, handing the pid to a notify closure nobody reads any more. The package already documents this steal within a single test: test 1 tolerates ECHILD from Output() because "the reap loop may collect the direct child before Output's own wait does". The same steal across a test boundary is unhandled, and it would only manifest when both tests share a binary, which is what CI does and what a -run filter hides. HYPOTHESIS REFUTED the same day, recorded so it is not re-derived: a probe started a ReapLoop with a full 8-deep SIGCHLD buffer, cancelled its context, then orphaned a zombie and checked whether the cancelled loop took it. Zero steals in 30 runs. The reason is structural rather than lucky - with ctx.Done() and buffered sigchld both ready, select picks uniformly at random, so the loop drains its buffer and returns after roughly two iterations, i.e. microseconds, while the orphan does not exist until exec.Command has run. The steal window cannot account for a 3-second failure. So the cause is UNKNOWN. Ruled out so far: a SIGCHLD lost before signal.Notify (the entry drain plus a 500ms ticker give about six chances inside the deadline), and a cross-test steal by a cancelled ReapLoop. Local reproduction stands at 260 clean runs: 40 isolated, 40 whole-package, 150 under GOMAXPROCS=2 with CPU contention, 30 probe. Next step is instrumentation, not a fix: make the test report why the wait failed - the Wait4 errno, whether the pid still exists, and its /proc state - so the next CI occurrence is diagnostic instead of a bare deadline. Note this is the third flake found in one day, after GOBLIN-DIV-037 and GOBLIN-DIV-038, but unlike those two its mechanism is not yet established. MEASURED RATE, and the most actionable fact here: gapi's Full Build and Test ran five times in CI on 2026-07-30 (30538360097, 30539163089, 30539907740, 30542246977, 30543372729) and failed once, about 20 percent, against 0 failures in 260 local runs. A defect that reproduces at one in five on a GitHub runner and never here is ENVIRONMENTAL, not a scheduling race - which is why adding CPU contention and pinning GOMAXPROCS=2 found nothing. Suspect what differs about the runner's process tree rather than the code's timing: PID namespace, an ancestor that is already a child subreaper, or how the Actions runner supervises and reparents orphans of the test binary. PR-27's failure and PR-28's pass are the same commit content on the same day, which isolates the variable to the runner. SECOND OCCURRENCE 2026-08-01, run 30697874470, on pull request 35 (div-046-stop-adopted): "pre-existing zombie 28564 not drained" - same test, same assertion, same 3s deadline. That pull request changes core/agentmgr and divergence.jsonl and touches core/subreaper not at all, so as with the first occurrence nothing in the diff can account for it. The job passed on rerun of the identical commit, which is the flake's signature. PID PROXIMITY, a new observation and the first fact here that points anywhere: the first failure named zombie 28560 (2026-07-30), this one 28564 (2026-08-01). Four apart, two days and two runner VMs apart. GitHub runners boot fresh and deterministically, so the test binary's children land at near-identical PIDs on every run. That is not a cause, but it corroborates the ENVIRONMENTAL reading over a scheduling race - a timing race would not concentrate on a PID - and it sharpens the instrumentation this exit already requires: record the zombie's own PID alongside the Wait4 errno and /proc state, because if the collision is with something else in the runner's process tree, that something is probably at a near-deterministic PID too. RATE CORRECTED, and the correction matters because the old number was this entry's most actionable claim. The recorded "about 20 percent" came from five Full Build and Test runs on a single day. Measured across the window instead: the job ran 24 times between 2026-07-30 and 2026-08-01 with one job-level failure still recorded, plus this occurrence - two known occurrences in about 25 attempts, roughly 8 percent rather than 20. The conclusion is unchanged and the signal is weaker: still far too rare to reproduce on demand, still zero in 260 local runs. MEASUREMENT TRAP, and the reason this had to be written down the day it happened: rerunning a failed job REPLACES its conclusion. A flake rerun to green vanishes from the run history - run 30697874470 now reports Full Build and Test as passing. Any failure rate derived from run history is therefore a LOWER BOUND, and the true rate is unrecoverable after the fact, which means the 24-run denominator above is itself only as good as the reruns nobody recorded. Occurrences of this flake must be appended here when observed. THIRD OCCURRENCE 2026-08-01, run 30710813750, on pull request 45 (div-049-shared-limits): "pre-existing zombie 28666 not drained", same test, same assertion. That pull request moves a limits parser between core/cgroups, core/schema and core/agentmgr and touches core/subreaper not at all - core/cgroups passed in the same run - so as with the first two, nothing in the diff can account for it. The failed job was rerun and passed on the identical commit. PID PROXIMITY, WEAKENED - this corrects the inference recorded with the second occurrence. That entry noted zombie 28560 (2026-07-30) and 28564 (2026-08-01) were four apart and reasoned that a near-deterministic runner boot made the collision target near-deterministic too. The third is 28666, about a hundred higher and on the same day as the second, so the PIDs cluster in a BAND rather than landing on a point and the sharper claim does not survive three data points. What remains is weaker and still useful: three sightings across two days all fall in 28.5k-28.7k, far tighter than chance over the pid space, which still points at a reproducible runner process tree rather than at timing. The instrumentation this exit requires should record the pid, so a fourth point can decide whether the band is stable or drifting upward. THE MEASUREMENT TRAP, NOW DEMONSTRATED RATHER THAN PREDICTED. The second occurrence recorded that rerunning a failed job REPLACES its conclusion, making any rate derived from run history a lower bound. This occurrence proves it: the failure was read out of the log and written down before the rerun, and run 30710813750 now reports Full Build and Test as SUCCESS - verified after the fact. Nothing in GitHub's history records that it ever failed. Three known occurrences exist only because they were transcribed here at the moment they happened, and the true rate is unrecoverable at any later date. INSTRUMENTED 2026-08-01, still open. ReapLoopWithObserver reports every Wait4 outcome - trigger, pid, status, errno - to an optional observer, and both tests now dump on the failure path: this process's child subreaper flag, whether the orphan is still in /proc, its state and parent pid, everything delivered to notify, and the full wait4 event log. A nil observer leaves the loop's control flow exactly as it was, deliberately: instrumentation that perturbs the timing of an intermittent failure can spend the failure without explaining it. Verified by breaking drain() so it never waits, running the test red, and reading the dump; restored byte-identical. HEALTHY BASELINE, recorded so the CI failure has something to diff against: the zombie is collected by the STARTUP drain as event 0 (pid=<orphan> status=exited(3) err=nil), event 1 is ECHILD, and every later event is a tick returning ECHILD. A healthy run produces NO sigchld-triggered events at all, because the startup drain already got it - so a failure showing sigchld events, or showing ECHILD at event 0, is already discriminating, as is a state other than Z or a ppid that is not ours. The flag is read by prctl in test code rather than beside BecomeSubreaper: PR_GET_CHILD_SUBREAPER needs unsafe, that is gapi's only hand-written unsafe, and putting it in the package would force a repo-wide gosec G103 exclude - muting a rule with zero findings for the sake of a diagnostic. The flag is not exposed in /proc (checked), so prctl is the only read path. FOURTH OCCURRENCE 2026-08-02, run 30734906746, on a PUSH TO MAIN at 9f9f113 - the ledger-only merge of pull request 55 - so main was left red by a flake on a documentation commit. Same test, same assertion: 'pre-existing zombie 28518 not drained'. As with the first three, nothing in the diff can account for it. THE INSTRUMENTATION PAID OFF AND THIS OCCURRENCE IS DIAGNOSTIC, the first that is. Captured: self pid 28504; self child_subreaper TRUE; orphan 28518 GONE from /proc, reaped by somebody and not delivered to notify; delivered to notify (0), the loop reaped nothing at all; and seven wait4 events, event 0 startup and events 1-6 tick, EVERY ONE returning ECHILD. Read against the healthy baseline recorded above - event 0 collects the orphan with status=exited(3) err=nil, event 1 ECHILD, no sigchld-triggered events - the failure differs on precisely the axis that baseline named as discriminating: ECHILD AT EVENT 0. Four facts together. (a) child_subreaper is true, so BecomeSubreaper did its job; not a flag failure. (b) wait4(-1) returns ECHILD at startup and on all six ticks across the whole 3-second window, and ECHILD from wait4(-1) means this process has NO CHILDREN AT ALL - not none ready, none existing. (c) Zero sigchld-triggered events; nothing was ever delivered. (d) The orphan is gone from /proc, so somebody else reaped it. CONCLUSION: THE ORPHAN NEVER ENTERED THIS PROCESS'S CHILD SET. ReapLoop did not misbehave - it correctly reported having no children, seven times. This is a REPARENTING failure, not a reaping failure. HYPOTHESES ELIMINATED, all of which presupposed the orphan arrived and was then mishandled, and none of which can produce ECHILD at event 0 with the subreaper flag set: a SIGCHLD lost before signal.Notify; a cross-test steal by a cancelled ReapLoop (already probe-refuted, now doubly so); any scheduling race inside the loop; any timing relationship between the startup drain and the ticker. This also rules out the fixes that were previously plausible - bounding the loop's goroutine, or changing drain/ticker timing, would now be fixing a mechanism that has been eliminated. WHAT SURVIVES is the environmental reading this entry has carried since its rate analysis, now with evidence rather than inference: the orphan is reparented somewhere other than this process, despite this process being a child subreaper. That is answerable, and it is the next INSTRUMENTATION step rather than a fix - record the orphan's ppid at the moment the intermediate exits, and the child-subreaper flag of each ancestor up the chain. If a nearer ancestor on the runner carries PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER it takes the orphan and reaps it, and the test's premise - that an orphan in our subtree comes to us - is false on that host. The same run's log shows the runner's cgroup path as system.slice/hosted-compute-agent.service, so the Actions runner's own supervision is the first candidate. MEASUREMENT TRAP, THIRD DEMONSTRATION: this failure was transcribed before any rerun, and main went green on the next commit (e72f348) without run 30734906746 ever being rerun. Four known occurrences; the denominator remains unrecoverable, so the rate stays a lower bound. SECOND INSTRUMENTATION PASS 2026-08-02, still open - a fix is still not being attempted, because the fourth occurrence eliminated every mechanism this entry carried and named no replacement. WHAT THE FIRST PASS COULD NOT SEE: every field it records is read AFTER the deadline, and the fourth occurrence found the orphan already GONE from /proc at that moment, so the facts that would say what happened to it - whether it was ever ours, and if not whose it was - had been destroyed roughly three seconds before anything looked. THE WAIT4 LOG ALONE IS NOT DISCRIMINATING, and this is demonstrated rather than argued: forcing every Wait4 in drain() to return ECHILD reproduces the fourth occurrence's event log EXACTLY - seven events, event 0 startup and events 1-6 tick, every one ECHILD, 'delivered to notify (0)' - while the orphan sits in /proc the entire time as a zombie whose ppid is ours. A broken reap loop and an orphan that never arrived produce the same seven lines, so the first pass's central artifact cannot by itself support the conclusion drawn from it. ADDED: (a) orphanTrace probes, /proc snapshots of the orphan taken on the HAPPY path while the answer still exists - one in each test at 'intermediate exited', immediately after Output() has waited for the shell so reparenting has already happened, and a second in the zombie test after its 200ms sleep, the two bracketing the window in which no reap loop is running and anything happening to the orphan is therefore not ours; (b) the /proc ancestor chain of the test process, each level with pid, comm and ppid; (c) the resolved path of the sh the orphan is spawned from. PROBE BASELINE ON A HEALTHY HOST, recorded so a CI dump has something to diff against: both tests read '<pid> (sh) state=Z ppid=<self>' at 'intermediate exited' - the orphan is already a zombie AND already ours by the time Output() returns - and the zombie test's second probe is identical. The three failure readings are therefore distinct. GONE at the first probe means somebody reaped it before this process was ever a candidate, and no reparenting failure occurred at all. A ppid that is not ours means reparenting went elsewhere, which is the hypothesis the fourth occurrence left standing. Present-and-ours at both probes together with ECHILD at event 0 is self-contradictory and indicts the measurement rather than the code, most likely the pid read from the shell's $!. THE FIRST READING IS A HYPOTHESIS THIS ENTRY DID NOT HAVE. 'The intermediate reaped its own background job before exiting' fits the fourth occurrence's evidence exactly - ECHILD at event 0, zero sigchld events, orphan absent from /proc - and involves no reparenting failure whatsoever, so the REPARENTING FAILURE conclusion recorded with that occurrence is one of two readings consistent with the evidence rather than the only one. It is a claim about which sh runs, which is why the resolved path is now dumped. Locally it is /nix/store/<hash>-bash-5.3p15/bin/sh, and CI runs the tests through 'nix develop -c mage -v test', so the devshell SHOULD make this hermetic and identical - the point of dumping it is that this is currently an inference from the workflow file, and a differing path in a CI dump would itself be the finding. surface: core/crypto/crypto.go (SavePrivate), core/crypto/age.go (WriteAgeIdentity)
violation: Private key material is written non-atomically, so a window exists in which it is on disk at a mode the operator did not intend. Two instances, one reachable and one not. (1) SavePrivate creates through safeio.CreatePrivate at 0600, writes the PEM, then chmods to 0600. The create mode only applies when the file does not already exist, so the chmod is what covers an overwrite - and it runs AFTER pem.Encode. Regenerating a key over a path that already holds a loose file leaves the key readable for the duration of the write. This is the residue of the 0644 fix (b5d5cf3), which closed the common case: a fresh path is 0600 from the moment it exists. (2) WriteAgeIdentity (age.go) writes an age identity - a real secret - with os.WriteFile at 0600, and os.WriteFile's perm argument likewise applies only on create. It has the same overwrite weakness and no compensating chmod at all. It has no caller in the current CLI, which is why it was left alone rather than changed blind. Neither is exploitable without a local attacker already watching the target path, but the whole point of the 0600 is that such an attacker is the threat.
rule: onboard/go-project-manifesto - assume hostile inputs, least privilege; found while fixing the 0644 defect in b5d5cf3
exit: RESOLVED 2026-08-01. Closes on the GATE the exit specified - a held descriptor, not a mode assertion - demonstrated failing. THE FIX: safeio.ReplaceOwnerOnly writes to a temp file in the destination's OWN directory (same directory because rename is only atomic within a filesystem), syncs, closes, and os.Rename's it into place; os.CreateTemp opens O_EXCL at 0600 and umask can only clear bits, so the data is owner-only from the instant it exists. Replacing rather than writing through is the load-bearing part: a replaced destination has no old mode to inherit, so the pre-existing-file case stops being special. SavePrivate (pem.EncodeToMemory) and WriteAgeIdentity both route through it, as does SavePublic - not named in this entry and not a secret, but included because this exit's own reviewer check is that the helper is the only 0600-creating path in core/crypto, which SavePublic would have failed. Its 0600 is preserved exactly; whether a public key should be 0600 is a separate question. Verified: `grep -n '0o\?600' core/crypto/*.go` excluding tests returns nothing. safeio.CreatePrivate is DELETED. It had exactly one caller - the function this entry names - and it is the footgun the residual warned about: a 0600-creating helper whose mode silently does not apply on overwrite, with that weakness written into its own doc comment as a caller obligation. Leaving it beside the correct helper is an invitation, not a mitigation. It is named for its guarantee rather than its action, because the bug closed here came from safeio.Create versus CreatePrivate, where the name said what the call did and not what it promised. THE GATE: TestSavePrivateReplacesRatherThanWritesThrough and TestWriteAgeIdentityReplacesRatherThanWritesThrough plant a 0644 file at the target path, hold an open descriptor on it, save, and require the descriptor to still read the OLD content - true only if the file was replaced. Proven by giving ReplaceOwnerOnly a write-through body: BOTH gate tests fail and the held descriptor reads back the actual PEM private key and the actual age secret key, which is the exposure this entry describes. In that same run TestSavePrivateIsOwnerOnly and TestSavePrivateTightensAnExistingLooseFile still PASSED - the pre-existing mode assertions cannot see the window, which is exactly why they never caught it. Restored byte-identical; 24 packages ok, 0 failures, lint clean, and green under GOWORK=off -mod=vendor, the mode CI resolves. DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: no directory fsync. rename(2) closes the mode-visibility race in the running kernel and a dirsync adds nothing to that property; it buys crash durability of the rename, which is a different concern with no ledger backing. The data Sync before the rename is kept and is not optional - without it a crash can surface the renamed file at zero length, which reads as key corruption rather than a clean rollback. If crash-durable key writes are wanted, that is its own entry. WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS SILENTLY FALSE AGAIN, unchanged from the original exit and not claimed as fixed: nothing structurally stops a future function in core/crypto from writing a secret with os.WriteFile. Deleting CreatePrivate removes the tempting wrong helper but adds no enforcement. The package is clean by grep today, and a grep is not a gate. A second residual, smaller: on failure the gate tests print the PEM and the age secret key into the log. Both are ephemeral generated test keys so nothing is exposed, but it is not a habit to spread to a test handling a real key.

surface: core/agentmgr/go_agent.go (Stop), core/agentmgr/python_agent.go (Stop), core/agentmgr/checkpoint.go (adopt)
violation: A CRIU-restored agent cannot be stopped, and the failure is silent. adopt() records the restored pid in adoptedPid and sets cmd to nil - deliberately, and its own comment says why: 'leaving a stale cmd in place would let Stop signal a pid that no longer belongs to this agent - exactly the recycling hazard the epoch guard exists to prevent.' But both Stop implementations open with `if a.cmd == nil || a.cmd.Process == nil { return nil }`, so for an adopted process Stop returns nil having done nothing. The caller sees success. The agent keeps running. The ABA hazard was avoided by converting the operation into a no-op, which trades a signal-safety defect for a liveness one and reports neither. adoptedPid is read in exactly one place, Pid(), so nothing else compensates. This is the one place in gapi where a bare PID with no os.Process handle exists, which is precisely where core/procsig's epoch guard is the only available protection - and gapi calls procsig zero times today. Found while restating GAPI-DIV-016 on 2026-08-01; the restore path landed under GOBLIN-DIV-018 and its stop half was never written.
rule: go-project-manifesto (fail loudly at boundaries; a function that cannot perform its contract must say so, not return nil); research/global-uuid-based-process-identity DDR-5 (delivery to a PID the caller does not hold a handle for needs the start_epoch guard)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-08-01. Closes on the gate, demonstrated failing. THE FIX: adopt() captures the start epoch via procsig.StartEpoch AT ADOPT TIME and stores it beside adoptedPid; Stop routes an adopted process through procsig.Signal with that STORED epoch. The ordering is the whole guard - reading the epoch at Stop time would compare the process to itself and could never fail. A failed capture leaves adoptedEpoch at zero and propagates the error from Restore, so a later Stop is refused rather than signalling blind. adopt() now returns an error. This is gapi's first caller of procsig, and the only place in the repo holding a bare pid with no os.Process handle - see GAPI-DIV-016 as restated, where the child paths are guarded by the Go runtime's pidfd handle instead. ERROR SEMANTICS, decided rather than defaulted: ErrProcessGone is SUCCESS - Stop's contract is that the process is not running, and it is not. ErrStaleEpoch is an ERROR: the supervisor is discovering its own record was false, having never observed the exit, published no status for it and run no cleanup, so reporting 'stopped' would assert an action that never happened. It publishes FAILED, matching what the child exit watcher publishes for an exit the supervisor did not initiate, and clears the recorded identity so nothing downstream acts on a pid that now belongs to a stranger. No retry, per procsig. A TRAP FOUND WHILE BUILDING IT: exit detection cannot rely on /proc/<pid>/stat being absent, because that entry survives for a ZOMBIE - a process that exited but has not been waited on. A wait loop polling only for ErrProcessGone spins against a corpse until its deadline. The check reads state and start epoch from ONE read (two reads could straddle an exit and pair a live state with a recycled epoch) and treats absent, state Z or X, or a changed epoch as gone. THE GATE: TestStopAdoptedProcessActuallyTerminatesIt adopts a live process the test owns, calls Stop, and asserts the process really terminated - the test owns the child so it can Wait, which sidesteps zombie detection in the assertion itself. Proven by removing only the adopted branch from GoAgent.Stop: the test fails with 'Stop reported success but the adopted process is still running', the defect stated as an assertion, while the PythonAgent subtest PASSES in the same run because only the Go path was reverted - the control showing the test measures the branch and not the weather. Restored byte-identical; uncached -race green, 24 packages 0 failures, lint clean, and green under GOWORK=off -mod=vendor. Both runners are covered: they are a parity contract and route through one shared helper. CORRECTION TO THIS ENTRY'S ORIGINAL EXIT, recorded rather than quietly dropped: it said to prove the stale-epoch path by letting the adopted process exit so the epoch no longer matches. That path is UNREACHABLE - an exited process yields ErrProcessGone, not ErrStaleEpoch. Reaching ErrStaleEpoch requires a LIVE process whose STORED epoch is wrong, and the test must additionally assert the process is still running afterwards, because the property being checked is that nothing was delivered. Implemented that way, with the ErrProcessGone case covered as its own test. WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS SILENTLY FALSE AGAIN: the epoch must stay captured at adopt time. Nothing structurally enforces that - moving the StartEpoch call into the stop path leaves every test green except the stale-epoch one, and a future test that adopts and stops in the same breath would not notice. Separately, NotifyExited matches agents by Pid() alone with no epoch to check against, so a recycled pid can match an adopted agent there too; that is the same class of hole one layer over and is not addressed here.

It reports EVERY violation in one error, since a gate that stops at the first hit turns one fix into N build cycles. surface: core/agentmgr/notify_exited.go (NotifyExited), core/agentmgr/go_agent.go and python_agent.go (Pid, adoptedPid lifetime)
violation: NotifyExited attributes a reaped pid to an agent by PID EQUALITY alone - it walks am.agents, takes the first whose Pid() matches, logs the exit under that agent's identity and returns. Its own doc comment calls the wait status recorded there 'the authoritative one, since the reaper may win the wait race', so this is a record claiming authority, not a debug line. For a spawned child the claim expires correctly: Pid() reads a.cmd.Process.Pid and cleanupAfterExit sets cmd to nil, so the agent stops claiming the pid once it exits. For an ADOPTED (CRIU-restored) process it does not. adoptedPid is cleared in exactly two places, both on the Stop path (adopted.go), so an adopted process that exits on its own leaves adoptedPid set and Pid() reports (adoptedPid, true) indefinitely. The agent goes on claiming a pid it no longer owns, and the next reap of that recycled pid is logged as that agent's exit with an authoritative wait status belonging to a stranger. GAPI-DIV-046 stored an adoptedEpoch that would distinguish the two, and NotifyExited cannot use it: by the time the reaper reports a pid the process is already reaped, so procsig.StartEpoch returns ErrProcessGone and there is no epoch left to compare. The obvious guard is unavailable at this seam, which is why this is its own entry rather than a follow-on to DIV-046. Called from gapi core/supervisor/pid1_wiring.go and from goblin internal/supervisor/pid1_wiring.go, so both PID-1 paths carry it.
rule: research/global-uuid-based-process-identity DDR-5 (a pid alone does not identify a process incarnation); go-project-manifesto (errors and records are data - a record that claims authority must be one)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-08-01. Closes on the CLAIM EXPIRING, demonstrated both ways. THE FIX: an adopted process gets an exit watcher that clears adoptedPid and adoptedEpoch, the way cleanupAfterExit clears cmd for a spawned child, so Pid() reports not-running and NotifyExited can no longer match it. No check was added at notification time, because none is possible - the process is already reaped when the pid arrives and /proc is gone, which is why this entry was written against claim expiry rather than verification. THE RESIDUAL THIS ENTRY NAMED WAS AVOIDED BY REUSE, NOT BY CARE. The exit warned that whatever watches for the exit is itself polling a pid and has the same recycling question one level down. The watcher calls the EXISTING adoptedHasExited from GAPI-DIV-046 rather than a second liveness check: one /proc/<pid>/stat read returning state and start epoch together, treating absent, Z, X, or a CHANGED EPOCH as gone. The epoch comparison therefore happens while the process still exists. Writing a fresh check would have reintroduced exactly the hole the entry predicted. THE WATCHER IS JOINABLE, not merely cancellable. GOBLIN-DIV-038 is open for the defect of goroutines that observe cancellation and are never waited for, and adding one here would have been careless. It terminates on three paths: it returns after firing; Stop detaches the handle under the lock and joins after unlocking; Reset joins on teardown. The locking rule is that stop() is never called with a.mu held, because onExit takes a.mu and joining under the lock would deadlock - every caller removes the handle from the field under the lock, making the join single-shot, then joins outside it. The Stop race resolves through the same `stopping` flag the child watcher uses, and adoptedExited re-checks the pid and epoch it was started on, so a re-adopt in flight cannot have its claim cleared by the watcher it replaced. An unattended adopted exit publishes FAILED, matching the child exit watcher for an exit the supervisor did not initiate. THE GATE: two tests over both runners. The first adopts a live process, lets it exit WITHOUT Stop, and polls for the claim to clear against a bounded deadline rather than sleeping a fixed duration - gapi already carries one unexplained flake in GAPI-DIV-043 and a second, self-inflicted, would be a poor trade for closing this. A Go agent is a single file named <name>.go.<type> declaring consts and lifecycle functions - no main, no flag parsing, no hand-written describe JSON, no signal handling. Referencing makes the Go compiler check the whole mapping, so a mishandled declaration is a build error in the author's file. THE RUNTIME LIVES IN adk/go/AGENT AND NEVER adk/go, as the entry demanded: gopy binds every exported symbol in adk/go into the Python ADK's native module, so a Run or Register there would leak this runtime into Python's C bindings. ALL THREE CONSEQUENCES CLOSED. (b) CONTROL EVENTS ARE EMITTED: the runtime sends starting, ready, stopping, stopped and error on stdout, which is the channel streamControl scans. 'ready' is what the supervisor turns into RUNNING and nothing else produces it, so a Go service can leave PENDING for the first time. Readiness waits out a grace period first, so an agent whose Start fails immediately reports error rather than announcing itself healthy - asserted, and discriminating on DURATION: the failing case returns in 0.00s where the healthy one takes the 250ms grace. Extras follow the lifecycle names and are de-duplicated, matching runner.py's dict.fromkeys. STDOUT IS FENCED. The author's stdout is redirected to stderr for the supervised path, because stdout is the control channel and a stray fmt.Println would otherwise be parsed as protocol. The Python runner fences the same way, so both languages give an author the same guarantee. Bounded deliberately: it moves the os.Stdout VARIABLE, not file descriptor 1, so cgo writing to the descriptor directly still reaches the channel. An exec'd child is NOT a gap - os/exec connects a nil Stdout to /dev/null. violation: There is no mount agent type, so the only filesystems gapi can mount are the six hardcoded in EarlyMounts. A deployment needing a data disk, a bind mount or an NFS share has nowhere to declare it, and no way to order an agent after it. systemd models this as a first-class unit type; gapi models it as a Go slice. THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS AND IS THE REASON THIS IS TRACTABLE: core/mounts has MountSpec{Source, Target, FSType, Flags, Options}, a Mounter interface with Mount/IsMounted/MkdirAll, and MountEarly which is idempotent over premounted targets and fails closed. What is missing is the agent kind, not the syscall surface. WHY IT IS A NEW KIND RATHER THAN A NEW TYPE STRING: every current Agent implementation supervises a PROCESS and derives liveness from process state. A mount has no pid, no stdout, no readiness handshake and no control events. Start is a syscall that returns immediately and 'active' is a STATE PREDICATE - is the target in mountinfo - which core/mounts already answers via IsMounted. AGREED SHAPE, operator 2026-08-02: a mount agent is CODE like any other, written in Go or Python, so the <name>.<lang>.<type> filename invariant holds unchanged. It is the socket pattern exactly: the agent DECLARES what the supervisor needs (Source, Target, FSType, Options, as a socket agent declares ListenStream), the SUPERVISOR performs the privileged operation (mount(2), as it binds and passes fd 3), and the agent's code runs against the result. That also removes the security objection to a declarative type: the supervisor mounts from metadata it can validate rather than from arbitrary agent code.
rule: cooperative-ecosystem-manifesto section 5 (the SDK's parity contract: a capability must be expressible in both languages with identical semantics); design/gapi-architecture.md (socket activation as the model for a privileged operation the supervisor owns and the agent consumes)
exit: A mount agent type discovered, ordered, started and stopped like any other, with these four decisions already taken and NOT to be relitigated. (1) START IS NOT REQUIRED for Type="mount". Register panics without Start today; that is relaxed for mounts rather than satisfied with a synthesized default, because if Start is always present its presence stops meaning anything. Absent Start makes 'this agent has post-mount work' visible in the source at a glance. (2) PARENT ORDERING IS DERIVED FROM Target, NEVER DECLARED. /var/lib/data implies /var/lib. This is what systemd does - nested mount points acquire BOTH a requirement and an ordering dependency automatically - and derived is strictly better than declared because a declared parent can be wrong while a derived one cannot. (3) ID MUST EQUAL THE ESCAPED Target: ID="var-lib-data" for Target="/var/lib/data". This is how duplicate mount points become unrepresentable rather than merely detected, and it costs no new mechanism: discovery is ALREADY first-ID-wins by agent ID, so two agents claiming one mount point collide as one ID and mask each other with the same override semantics as everything else. systemd gets this by requiring the unit filename to match Where=; gapi keeps <name>.<lang>.<type> and gets it from a field validation instead. (4) SYSTEM SCOPE ONLY. A mount agent in user scope is a privilege-escalation primitive unless confined to a user namespace, so a mount discovered in user scope is REFUSED with a reason rather than quietly skipped. This is the first real job for the Scope parameter beyond selecting directories. CLOSES ON: a test that declares a mount agent over a loopback or tmpfs target, asserts the supervisor mounted it (IsMounted true) before the agent's dependents start, and asserts reverse unmount at shutdown - run for BOTH languages, because a capability expressible in one is a parity break. DEMONSTRATED BY FAILURE: declare two agents with the same Target and show the second is masked rather than racing; and declare a mount in user scope and show it refused. EARLYMOUNTS IS DELIBERATELY OUT OF SCOPE and deferred by the operator. The finding that shapes it, recorded now so it is not rediscovered: HIERARCHY ORDERING IS INSUFFICIENT FOR THE EARLY SET. The table is /dev, /proc, /sys, /sys/fs/cgroup, /run, /tmp, and only cgroup2-after-/sys is a parent/child edge - /dev before /proc is declared sequence. So the early set cannot use the ordering rule a mount agent would, and it is a shared type with two drivers rather than a merge. The bootstrap constraint stands regardless: agent discovery reads a filesystem and execs binaries, so nothing can be discovered before /proc and /run exist. WRITE FIRST, whichever way that goes: a string-to-Flags parser test that parses the option string form of each of the six EarlyMounts and asserts it equals the hardcoded uintptr bitmask. Both answers need that parser, and the test either validates or falsifies the shared-vocabulary premise before any design rests on it. LATER, NOT NOW: systemd's RequiresMountsFor= - any unit naming a PATH and the supervisor resolving it to the mount agents covering that path, parents included. It is the generalisation worth stealing once the type exists.
